n: Being a good neighbor isn’t optional. If you see someone’s animal wandering off, you can’t look the other way — you must return it.
If the owner lives far away or is unknown, take the animal home and care for it until they come looking.
The same applies to donkeys, clothing, and anything else lost. Ignoring lost property is not allowed.

f.g: You may not shirk this duty.

n: If a neighbor’s animal has collapsed under its load, help lift it. Kindness extends to animals and to people in trouble.

Men and women must not wear clothing meant to present themselves as the opposite sex. Many scholars think pagan rituals involving cross-dressing were in view; the law upheld the distinction between men and women.

f.w: that which pertaineth unto a man
f.g: Can include a man’s gear or equipment, not just garments.

n: If you find a bird’s nest, you may take the eggs or chicks but not the mother bird along with them.
Let the mother go so she can breed again. Respecting life and its sources brings blessing. The same promise is attached to honoring parents.

f.w: that thou mayest prolong thy days

n: Flat roofs were living spaces, so a new house needed a railing. Failing to build one would make the owner responsible for any fall.

f.g: A parapet or low wall around a flat roof.

f.w: bring not blood upon thine house
f.g: Avoid bloodguilt for a death you could have prevented.

n: Don’t plant a second crop between the vines. The mixed produce would become “holy” — forfeited to the sanctuary.
Don’t yoke an ox and a donkey together. They differ in strength and gait, making it cruel to both. Paul drew a lesson about being unequally yoked.

f.w: plow with an ox and an ass together

n: No clothing woven from both wool and linen. Such mixtures were reserved for priestly garments, reminding Israel of the distinction between holy and common.
Tassels on the four corners of the outer cloak reminded Israelites to remember and keep God’s commandments.
A new section on marriage. It begins with a husband who turns against his new wife after the wedding.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for consummating the marriage.

n: He spreads a slanderous claim that she was not a virgin, trying to shame her and escape the marriage.

f.w: bring up an evil name upon her

n: Her parents could defend her before the elders with evidence from the wedding night.

f.w: the tokens of the damsel's virginity
f.g: Likely the bloodstained wedding cloth kept as proof.

n: Her father speaks up for her publicly.
The father presents the evidence to refute the false charge.
The lying husband was publicly punished.
He paid a heavy fine to her father and lost any right to divorce her, protecting her from abandonment and disgrace.

f.w: he may not put her away

n: But if the accusation proved true…
…the law treated it as a grave crime against her family and community. Such penalties reflect ancient Israel’s strict covenant code; the Savior later showed mercy and called sinners to repentance.

f.g: Committed a disgraceful act — a serious moral offense.

n: Adultery brought the death penalty on both parties under the law of Moses. Marriage was sacred and central to the covenant community.

f.w: they shall both of them die

n: A betrothed young woman was legally almost the same as a wife.
If it happened in a town, the law presumed she could have called for help and was consenting, so both were punished.

f.w: because she cried not, being in the city
f.g: Because she did not call for help where others could hear.

n: But if a man assaulted her in the countryside, only he was guilty.
The victim bore no guilt at all. The law compares the crime to murder — a violent attack on an innocent person.

f.w: there is in the damsel no sin

n: The law gave her the benefit of the doubt: she may have cried out with no one there to help.

f.w: there was none to save her
f.g: No one was there to rescue her.

n: A case involving an unengaged young woman.
The man had to pay a heavy bride-price and marry her if her father agreed (Exodus 22:17), with no right to divorce. In that society this protected her from being left without support.

f.g: A large sum, perhaps several years’ wages.

n: No man could marry his father’s wife (his stepmother). This verse is 23:1 in Hebrew Bibles.

f.g: An idiom: dishonor his father by uncovering what belongs to him.
